The basic structure is always the same idea, even if details differ by protocol. A packet has a
The header describes how the packet should be handled.

It contains metadata needed by the network. Typical header fields are source address, destination address, protocol identifier, packet length, and fields for control like time-to-live or hop count. Routers mostly look only at the header to decide where to send the packet next.
The payload is the actual data being carried.
This is what the application wants to send: part of a web page, a message, a file chunk, or anything else. The network does not care what the payload means, it just moves it.
The trailer is used for integrity checking.
At lower layers like Ethernet, the trailer often contains a
so the receiver can detect corruption caused by noise or interference.

Packet structure is layered. For example, an Ethernet frame contains an IP packet as its payload, and the IP packet contains a TCP segment, which contains application data. Each layer adds its own header. This is why packets grow as they move down the stack and shrink as headers are removed on receive.

The key point is that a packet is self-describing. Every packet carries enough information for the network to route it and for the receiver to interpret it correctly, without relying on a permanent connection.

In HTTP/1.1, each request/response pair required a new TCP connection, which incurred the overhead of establishing and tearing down a new connection for each request/response. This meant that the number of round trips required to load a web page could have a significant impact on the page's overall load time

To mitigate this issue, HTTP/1.1 introduced the concept of persistent connections, which allowed multiple requests and responses to be sent and received over the same TCP connection. This reduced the number of round trips required to load a web page, improving its overall performance
However, even with persistent connections, HTTP/1.1 was still sensitive to RTT because it only allowed a
to be outstanding at a time. This meant that if a request took a long time to complete, subsequent requests would have to wait before they could be sent
